drills.los_text: discuss asset size, liquidity needs, time horizon, and regulatory or other considerations as constraints on asset allocation

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely one of the four common constraints considered when modeling asset allocation alternatives?

options.A: The number of asset classes in the strategic policy universe.
options.B: Asset size.
options.C: Liquidity needs.

rationales.A: The four constraints are asset size, liquidity needs, time horizon, and regulatory or other external considerations; taxes are treated separately under the tax LOS. The number of asset classes in the strategic policy universe is not itself a constraint — it is an output shaped by the constraints, since the size, liquidity, horizon and regulatory limits are what determine how wide a usable opportunity set can be.
rationales.B: Asset size is one of the four. It binds in both directions: a very small portfolio cannot reach the minimums or support the due diligence that some asset classes demand, and a very large one can exhaust the capacity of the managers in a strategy.
rationales.C: Liquidity needs are one of the four. They have to be weighed against the liquidity characteristics of the asset classes in the opportunity set, and integrating those two sides is an essential element of investment planning.

questions.stem: Research on defined benefit pension plan size and performance from 1990 to 2008 found that large DB plans outperformed smaller plans on a risk-adjusted basis by most likely:

options.A: 10–15 basis points per year.
options.B: 45–50 basis points per year.
options.C: 100–200 basis points per year.

rationales.A: This understates the measured advantage. Dyck and Pomorski (2011) put the risk-adjusted advantage of large DB plans over smaller ones at 45–50 basis points per year, not 10–15.
rationales.B: Dyck and Pomorski (2011) found that large DB plans outperformed smaller ones by 45–50 basis points per year on a risk-adjusted basis. The gains come from a combination of cost savings related to internal management, greater ability to negotiate fees with external managers, and the ability to support larger allocations to private equity and real estate. This is the evidence behind the claim that asset owners, unlike investment managers, exhibit increasing returns to scale.
rationales.C: This overstates the measured advantage. A risk-adjusted edge of 1%–2% per year from size alone would dwarf the cost and access advantages actually documented; the figure is 45–50 basis points per year.

questions.stem: A US$25 billion fund plans to allocate 5% of its assets to global small-cap equity across three to four active managers, each of which can manage about US$1.3 billion effectively. The allocation most likely:

options.A: leaves each manager's asset base essentially unchanged.
options.B: takes advantage of small-cap equity's high scalability.
options.C: concentrates an undesirably large share of each manager's assets in one client.

rationales.A: The composition of each manager's asset base is materially affected. The allocation is US$1.25 billion, which is US$300–400 million per manager across three or four managers — 23%–31% of an effective asset base of roughly US$1.3 billion. A single client of that weight changes the manager's business, not just its holdings.
rationales.B: Small-cap equity is one of the strategies most sensitive to diseconomies of scale, not one of the most scalable. Above some size, active small-cap strategies become difficult to deploy effectively, because position limits and liquidity in small-cap names cap how much capital the strategy can absorb. That is why effective capacity here is only about US$1.3 billion per manager.
rationales.C: 5% of US$25 billion is US$1.25 billion, or US$300–400 million per manager across three or four managers. Against an effective capacity of about US$1.3 billion, that single client would be 23%–31% of the manager's assets under management. This is an undesirable operational risk for both sides: the asset owner's relationship dominates the manager's book, and a future redemption would be disruptive to the manager and to the remaining clients. Above some size, active investment strategies become difficult to deploy effectively.

questions.stem: Owners of very large portfolios frequently choose to invest passively in developed equity markets. The most likely reason is that:

options.A: their long horizons make active alpha irrelevant.
options.B: their size inhibits alpha potential in those markets.
options.C: index funds supply liquidity that active strategies cannot.

rationales.A: A long horizon does not make alpha irrelevant, and these owners do pursue active strategies — in private equity, hedge funds, and infrastructure. Nor is passive the default for every asset class. The passive choice in developed equities is size-driven.
rationales.B: Owners of very large portfolios face size constraints in allocating to active equity strategies. They frequently invest passively in developed equity markets, where their size inhibits alpha potential: the capital they would need to put to work exceeds what active developed-market strategies can absorb without eroding the edge. Finite governance resources can then be allocated toward such strategies as private equity, hedge funds, and infrastructure, where scale and resources instead provide a competitive advantage.
rationales.C: Liquidity is not the rationale. Active developed-market equity strategies are themselves liquid, so there is no liquidity gap for indexing to close. The logic is that size inhibits alpha potential in developed equities, so finite governance resources are redirected to strategies where scale and resources provide a competitive advantage.

questions.stem: As assets under management grow, investment managers most likely incur disadvantages including:

options.A: narrower opportunity sets imposed by regulatory position limits.
options.B: smaller trade sizes that reduce price impact.
options.C: larger trade sizes, style drift from inflows, and slower decision making.

rationales.A: Regulatory position limits are a separate constraint, not among the disadvantages of manager scale identified here. Those disadvantages are price impact from larger trades, style drift driven by capital inflows, and organizational complexity.
rationales.B: Trade sizes grow with assets under management rather than shrink, so price impact rises as the manager gets larger. The direction stated here is the opposite of the effect.
rationales.C: Growth in assets under management leads to larger trade sizes and therefore greater price impact; capital inflows may lead active managers to pursue ideas outside their core investment theses; and organizational hierarchies may slow decision making and reduce incentives. Asset owners, in contrast, are found to have increasing returns to scale — which is why size helps the owner and hurts the manager.

questions.stem: For an asset owner with a small portfolio, such as a US$250 million university endowment with limited governance resources, the most appropriate asset allocation most likely emphasizes:

options.A: large and liquid asset classes, with limited commingled alternatives.
options.B: a single asset class, to reduce complexity.
options.C: large allocations to hedge funds, private equity, and infrastructure.

rationales.A: Asset size and limited governance resources are both significant constraints at this scale. The allocation should emphasize large and liquid investments — cash equivalents, developed and emerging market equity, sovereign and investment-grade bonds. Some small portion could be allocated to commingled real estate, private equity, or hedge fund vehicles, but only after ensuring that the board has the necessary expertise or engages an outside expert.
rationales.B: Concentrating in a single asset class would forfeit the diversification benefit, and complexity is not the binding problem: broad diversification across liquid asset classes is available to a small portfolio cheaply through pooled vehicles and demands little governance capacity.
rationales.C: Large allocations to hedge funds, private equity, and infrastructure ignore the size and governance constraints. A US$250 million portfolio runs into minimum commitment sizes, the cost of manager due diligence, and the board expertise needed to sustain such a program through a full cycle.

questions.stem: The two dimensions of liquidity that must be considered in asset allocation are most likely:

options.A: the asset owner's liquidity needs and the asset classes' liquidity characteristics.
options.B: the size of the portfolio and the size of the asset class.
options.C: the historical bid–ask spread and turnover.

rationales.A: Two dimensions must be considered: first, the liquidity needs of the asset owner, and second, the liquidity characteristics of the asset classes in the opportunity set. Integrating the two is an essential element of successful investment planning, because an asset class is only as usable as the owner's own cash demands allow.
rationales.B: Portfolio size and asset class size belong to the asset size constraint, not to liquidity as such. Size affects which asset classes are reachable and whether manager capacity is exhausted; it says nothing about how fast a holding can be converted to cash or what the owner's cash needs are.
rationales.C: Bid–ask spreads and turnover are important measures of how liquid an asset class is, but they capture only the asset side of the question. The owner's own liquidity needs are the other dimension, and historical spreads also understate stress-period costs.

questions.stem: A bank's day-to-day operations portfolio most likely requires:

options.A: concentration in long-dated infrastructure.
options.B: large allocations to private equity.
options.C: high-quality, very short-term, highly liquid assets.

rationales.A: Long-dated infrastructure is inappropriate for a day-to-day operations portfolio, which turns over constantly and must be convertible to cash on demand. Such holdings would belong, if anywhere, in a bank's longer-term investment portfolio.
rationales.B: Private equity is inappropriate for a day-to-day operations portfolio. Locking up capital to harvest an illiquidity premium is directly at odds with a very high need for liquidity, and the capital commitments themselves create further calls on cash.
rationales.C: A bank's day-to-day operations portfolio will typically experience very high turnover and a very high need for liquidity; therefore the investment portfolio must hold high-quality, very short-term, and highly liquid assets. Longer-term bank investment portfolios, which fund no immediate operational demands, may allocate more to less liquid investments.

questions.stem: In the 2008–2009 global financial crisis, illiquidity became a substantial problem for asset owners most likely because:

options.A: owners could not sell even their government bonds.
options.B: owners sold their most liquid assets first, raising the illiquid share.
options.C: owners sold their least liquid assets first, leaving mostly cash.

rationales.A: The most liquid assets, such as government bonds, remained saleable throughout — which is precisely why owners sold them first. The problem arose from that behavior, not from an inability to sell anything at all.
rationales.B: When investors liquidated their most liquid assets to meet financial obligations, or to raise cash in fear of further declines, the remaining less liquid assets became an ever-larger portion of a shrinking portfolio. The illiquid allocation was never increased deliberately; it rose because the denominator fell and only the saleable assets left. Many investors were then forced to sell private partnership interests on the secondary market at steeply discounted prices; others defaulted on outstanding private fund capital commitments. This is why the owner's own liquidity needs, and not just the liquidity characteristics of each asset class, have to be built into the allocation in advance.
rationales.C: This reverses the mechanism. Owners sold their most liquid holdings first to meet obligations, which left illiquid assets an ever-larger share of shrinking portfolios; the forced sales of private partnership interests at steeply discounted secondary prices came only afterward, out of necessity. Portfolios ended up illiquid, not concentrated in cash.

questions.stem: Panic selling of illiquid positions during the 2008–2009 global financial crisis, by governance groups lacking the mental fortitude to hold them, most likely resulted in:

options.A: temporary underperformance that fully reversed.
options.B: permanent losses in wealth.
options.C: no lasting effect on wealth.

rationales.A: The effect is permanent, not temporary. The rebound in returns does not restore the wealth given up, because the assets that would have earned the recovery were sold before it arrived.
rationales.B: If those responsible for oversight lack the mental fortitude to maintain course through the crisis, illiquid investments are unlikely to produce their expected rewards. Rates of return may be mean-reverting, but wealth is not: losses resulting from panic selling during times of stress become permanent losses, because there are fewer assets left to earn returns in a post-crash recovery.
rationales.C: The effect on wealth is lasting. Selling into the decline leaves a smaller asset base to compound through the recovery, so the shortfall persists even after returns themselves revert to normal levels.

questions.stem: When central bank quantitative easing leaves markets with too much liquidity, the result is most likely:

options.A: higher asset valuations and eroded expected returns.
options.B: higher expected returns and greater risk compensation.
options.C: lower asset valuations and larger idle cash balances.

rationales.A: Overliquidity in a market tends to push asset valuations too high, because investors try to put their excess liquidity to work and bid up the price of whatever risk assets are available. Price paid and expected future return move in opposite directions, so the same flows that lift valuations erode the expected future returns of the asset classes being bought. Following the global financial crisis, and again during the COVID-19 pandemic, central banks pumped extra cash into the system through asset purchase and quantitative easing programs; that cash fueled the rebound in equity markets and pushed interest rates lower, leaving investors with richer current prices and thinner forward-looking return estimates.
rationales.B: The direction of the return effect is the reverse. Liquidity-driven buying raises current prices, and a higher price paid today lowers, rather than raises, the return expected from today forward. Excess liquidity chasing a limited supply of assets compresses risk premiums instead of increasing the compensation investors demand for bearing risk, which is why the post-crisis quantitative easing era is associated with lower prospective returns across asset classes rather than higher ones.
rationales.C: Investors do not leave excess liquidity sitting in cash balances; they put it to work, which bids valuations up rather than depressing them. The observed effect of the post-crisis and pandemic-era asset purchase programs was a rebound in equity markets and lower interest rates, that is, higher valuations on the assets investors were buying, not the cash-hoarding, low-valuation outcome described here.

questions.stem: A frozen pension plan may soon eliminate its pension obligation by purchasing a group annuity. For this plan, the most appropriate asset allocation approach is:

options.A: allocating heavily to illiquid assets.
options.B: increasing the equity allocation aggressively.
options.C: prioritizing the liquidity of plan assets.

rationales.A: A large allocation to illiquid assets ignores the plan's imminent liquidity need. If there is a significant probability that the sponsor will terminate the obligation through a group annuity purchase, assets have to be available at predictable value when that transaction is executed; holdings in private equity, direct real estate, or similar vehicles cannot be liquidated on demand, and forcing a sale would mean accepting a discount. The illiquidity premium is compensation for an ability to tie capital up over long horizons, which a plan facing a near-term termination event does not have.
rationales.B: Aggressively increasing equity exposure is inappropriate for a plan preparing to terminate. A frozen plan has no new accruals, a short and largely known liability stream, and a possible near-term funding event, so raising equity risk raises the chance that asset values fall just when the annuity premium has to be paid. At this stage risk reduction and liquidity, not return seeking, govern the allocation.
rationales.C: A frozen pension plan that may soon eliminate its pension obligation through the purchase of a group annuity must prioritize the liquidity of plan assets. If there is a significant probability that the company will take this step, liquidity becomes a primary concern, because a substantial allocation to illiquid assets may leave the plan sponsor unable to execute the desired annuity purchase at the time it is wanted or at an acceptable price. The plan therefore favors assets that can be converted to cash, or transferred to the insurer, at predictable value.

questions.stem: As an investor's human capital, which carries predominantly bond-like risk, declines over time, and assuming no change in the investor's utility function, the allocation of financial capital most likely shifts toward:

options.A: a larger allocation to equities.
options.B: a larger allocation to bonds.
options.C: an unchanged allocation.

rationales.A: This reverses the direction the framework implies. Human capital is the bond-like component of total wealth, so while it is large the financial portfolio can carry more equity and still leave the risk of total wealth at the investor's target. As human capital runs down, that bond-like ballast disappears and the financial portfolio has to supply it, which means a smaller equity weight over time, not a larger one.
rationales.B: Bodie, Merton, and Samuelson (1992) treat total wealth as human capital plus financial capital. Assuming no change in the investor's utility function, as human capital, with its predominantly bond-like risk, declines over time, the asset allocation for financial capital reflects an increasing allocation to bonds, so that the risk of total wealth stays consistent with the investor's preferences throughout life. This is the logic behind target-date fund glide paths, which move steadily toward bonds as the participant ages and the remaining stream of earnings shrinks.
rationales.C: The optimal allocation is not static, because one of its inputs is not static. Human capital shrinks as working years are used up, so the share of total wealth that is implicitly bond-like shrinks with it; holding the financial allocation constant would let the risk of total wealth drift upward over the investor's life, which is inconsistent with an unchanged utility function.

questions.stem: Under the random-walk return assumptions underlying mean-variance optimization, extending an investor's time horizon most likely means that:

options.A: shortfall probability falls, so time diversification holds.
options.B: returns become perfectly predictable.
options.C: risk is not reduced and outcome dispersion widens.

rationales.A: The classical intuition is disputed under a random walk. The probability of ending below a target may indeed decline as the horizon lengthens, but that is only one measure of risk, and treating it as proof of time diversification ignores the magnitude of the loss conditional on falling short. Samuelson (1963, 1969) showed that with serially independent returns there is no reduction in risk from a longer horizon, so time diversification does not hold as a general proposition.
rationales.B: Returns remain uncertain at every horizon. Under a random walk the variance of cumulative returns grows in proportion to the number of periods, and only the variance of the annualized average return shrinks. A long horizon therefore narrows the distribution of average annual outcomes while widening the distribution of terminal wealth; predictability never arrives.
rationales.C: Under the random walk assumption there is no reduction in risk from a longer time horizon. Although the probability of reduced wealth, or of falling short of a target, may be lower at longer horizons, the dispersion of possible outcomes, and hence the magnitude of a potential loss, widens as the horizon expands. In the illustration behind this result, the lower boundary of expected S&P 500 ending wealth at a 95% confidence interval is below the initial investment for every holding period shorter than 10 years, and does not exceed the ending wealth of the risk-free asset until 30 years.

questions.curriculum_ref: Time Horizon — time diversification of risk

questions.stem: Evidence that the returns on risky assets display mean-reverting tendencies over intermediate to long time horizons most likely supports:

options.A: more risk for long-horizon goals and less as horizons shorten.
options.B: the same allocation regardless of time horizon.
options.C: an all-cash allocation for every investor.

rationales.A: Although one-year returns are largely independent of one another, there is some evidence that risky asset returns can display mean-reverting tendencies over intermediate to longer time horizons. Mean reversion implies that a stretch of poor returns is more likely to be followed by better ones, which narrows the dispersion of long-horizon outcomes relative to the pure random walk case. That supports the conventional arguments for funding long-term goals with higher risk and return assets, and for reducing allocations to riskier assets as the time horizon shortens, which is the pattern embedded in glide paths and in goals-based allocation.
rationales.B: A constant allocation at every horizon is what a strict random walk, with no mean reversion and no change in the investor's circumstances, would justify. If returns mean revert, the risk of holding risky assets depends on how long they are held, so horizon becomes a relevant input and the allocation should be adjusted as that horizon shortens.
rationales.C: Mean reversion is an argument for taking risk over long horizons, not for avoiding it. An all-cash allocation would forgo the risk premium entirely and, for a long-horizon investor, introduces the larger danger of failing to keep pace with inflation and of not reaching the goal being funded.

questions.stem: Insurance companies typically hold the largest component of their asset base in fixed income, most likely in order to:

options.A: maximize liquidity for policyholder redemptions.
options.B: match assets to the cash flows of underwritten risks.
options.C: earn the highest expected return under book-value accounting.

rationales.A: Liquidity matters to an insurer, but it is not why fixed income dominates the balance sheet. The driver is liability matching: aligning asset cash flows with the projected probabilistic cash flows of the risks the company has underwritten, in both timing and amount. Insurers also hold return-seeking assets up to the limits regulation allows, so the portfolio is not constructed to maximize liquidity either.
rationales.B: Insurers are most often highly focused on matching assets to the projected probabilistic cash flows of the risks they underwrite, which makes fixed income the natural core of the portfolio and typically the largest component of an insurance company's asset base. Return-seeking assets are permitted but capped: regulatory limits on equity commonly run from a maximum of around 10% up to 30% in Switzerland and 50% in Mexico, while Israel and Korea impose 15% limits on real estate. Some regions also apply book-value accounting, which changes how asset price movements show up in reported results and reinforces the preference for instruments with contractual cash flows.
rationales.C: The accounting regime does not make fixed income the highest-returning asset class, and over long horizons it is not. Bonds dominate insurer portfolios because their cash flows match the projected probabilistic cash flows of underwritten risks; equity is permitted but limited, typically to a maximum of about 10% and up to 30% in Switzerland or 50% in Mexico, so the fixed-income weight reflects matching and regulation rather than a return ranking.

questions.curriculum_ref: Regulatory and Other External Constraints — Insurance Companies

questions.stem: Solvency II, the harmonized EU-wide insurance regulatory regime that took effect in January 2016, most likely:

options.A: caps equity holdings at a fixed share of assets for every insurer.
options.B: applies one flat capital ratio regardless of asset mix.
options.C: scales minimum capital to each insurer's assets, liabilities, and risk.

rationales.A: Solvency II sets no single fixed equity cap applying to all insurers. It works through risk-based capital charges that differ by asset class, so a given equity allocation absorbs more capital than a comparable bond allocation; that shapes, rather than fixes, each insurer's allocation, and the binding constraint depends on the insurer's own balance sheet. Hard percentage ceilings of the kind described here belong to other regimes, where equity limits typically range from a maximum of around 10% up to 30% in Switzerland or 50% in Mexico.
rationales.B: The regime is risk-based rather than flat. Minimum capital levels are set from the insurer's own mix of assets, liabilities, and risk, and asset classes are often treated differently for the purpose of determining whether the insurer meets its risk-based capital requirement. A uniform ratio applied irrespective of asset mix would defeat the purpose of harmonizing risk-based capital requirements, since two insurers with identical balance sheet size but very different risk could not be held to the same number.
rationales.C: Solvency II is an EU legislative program implemented in all 28 member states, including the United Kingdom, in January 2016, and it introduced a new harmonized EU-wide insurance regulatory regime designed to harmonize risk-based capital requirements. Minimum capital levels for insurers are set on the basis of the insurer's mix of assets, liabilities, and risk, and asset classes are often treated differently in determining whether an insurer meets those requirements. That drives distinct capital treatment of equities, bonds, real estate, and other exposures, and it feeds directly into the insurer's asset allocation decision.

questions.stem: Norway's sovereign wealth fund, NBIM, operates under an internal constraint that permits investment in only one alternative asset class, which is most likely:

options.A: real estate.
options.B: hedge funds.
options.C: private equity.

rationales.A: NBIM is not permitted to invest in any alternative asset class other than real estate, and that allocation is itself limited to no more than 7% of assets. The pattern is typical of sovereign wealth funds: as publicly owned entities they are subject to broad public scrutiny and tend to adopt a lower-risk asset allocation than their very long time horizons alone would justify, in order to avoid reputation risk.
rationales.B: Hedge funds fall outside the single alternative asset class NBIM is allowed to hold, so the exposure is excluded rather than unconstrained. Nothing in the mandate is unlimited: even the permitted alternative, real estate, is capped at no more than 7% of assets.
rationales.C: Private equity is not the alternative asset class NBIM is permitted to hold. Its mandate allows real estate only, and even that is limited to no more than 7% of assets, a conservative stance adopted by many publicly owned funds to limit reputation risk.

questions.stem: Sharia law, which is an example of a religious constraint on asset allocation, most likely prohibits investment in:

options.A: only securities denominated in foreign currencies.
options.B: all equity and fixed-income assets, whatever the underlying business.
options.C: businesses linked to pork, alcohol, tobacco, pornography, prostitution, gambling, or weaponry.

rationales.A: Currency of denomination is not the Sharia screen. The constraint runs to the nature of the underlying business and to the way returns are earned, not to where a security is issued or in what currency it is priced: a domestic security in a prohibited industry is excluded, and a foreign-currency security in a permitted business is not.
rationales.B: This is over-inclusive. Sharia law does not exclude equity and fixed income as asset classes; it excludes particular businesses and particular structures. Equity in a company with no prohibited activities is investable, while conventional interest-bearing debt is problematic because of the interest payment itself, which is why Sharia-compliant portfolios use sukuk and similar profit-sharing structures rather than abandoning fixed income altogether.
rationales.C: Sharia law prohibits investment in businesses with links to pork, alcohol, tobacco, pornography, prostitution, gambling, or weaponry. It further constrains investment in businesses that operate on interest payments, which takes in most major Western banks and mortgage providers, and in businesses that transfer risk, which takes in major Western insurers. Religious constraints of this kind are one instance of the broader set of values-based screens, with environmental, social, and governance considerations becoming increasingly important to institutional and individual investors alike.

questions.stem: Pension funds are subject to a wide array of jurisdiction-specific investment constraints. One such constraint is most likely that:

options.A: Switzerland bars pension funds from holding real estate.
options.B: Canada caps investment in any one entity at thirty percent of market value.
options.C: Japan requires a minimum share of assets in Japanese bonds for tax-exempt status.

rationales.A: Switzerland does not prohibit pension fund real estate; it permits the holding and generally limits it to a maximum of 30% of assets. The constraint is a ceiling rather than an exclusion, and real estate is an ordinary allocation for Swiss plans.
rationales.B: The Canadian limit is 10%, not the higher figure stated here: investment in any one entity, or in a group of related entities, is capped at 10% of market value. The rule is a concentration limit intended to force diversification across issuers, so overstating it by a factor of three would permit exactly the concentrations the regime is written to prevent.
rationales.C: Japanese pension funds must hold a certain minimum percentage of assets in Japanese bonds in order to maintain their tax-exempt status, which constrains directly how much of the portfolio can be allocated elsewhere. It sits alongside a wide array of other jurisdiction-specific rules: Canada allows a maximum of 10% of market value in any one entity or group of related entities; Switzerland generally limits real estate to 30% of assets; Estonia allows a maximum of 75% in public equity with no limit on foreign investment; Brazil allows a maximum of 70% in public equity with no more than 10% in foreign public equity; and Ukraine limits bonds to 40%.

drills.los_text: discuss tax considerations in asset allocation and rebalancing

questions.stem: The expected after-tax return for an asset whose return is purely interest income is most likely:

options.A: The pre-tax return divided by one minus the tax rate.
options.B: The pre-tax return plus the tax rate.
options.C: The pre-tax return multiplied by one minus the tax rate.

rationales.A: Dividing by (1 − t) inverts the adjustment and pushes the after-tax return above the pre-tax return: for a 3% coupon taxed at 40%, it would give 0.03 / (1 − 0.40) = 0.05, or 5.00%, which is higher than the 3% actually earned before tax. Tax is a drag, so the pre-tax return has to be multiplied by (1 − t), not divided by it.
rationales.B: Adding the tax rate treats tax as something the investor receives rather than pays, and treats it as an additive constant rather than a proportion of the return. The tax drag on interest income is proportional to the income itself: a 3% coupon taxed at 40% loses 0.03 × 0.40 = 0.012, or 1.20 percentage points, leaving 1.80%, not 3% plus anything.
rationales.C: Expected after-tax return is r_at = r_pt × (1 − t), where r_at is the expected after-tax return, r_pt is the expected pre-tax return, and t is the expected tax rate. Interest income is taxed annually at the investor's ordinary income rate, with no deferral and no preferential rate, so the full return is reduced proportionally. For a 3% coupon bond held by an investor facing a 40% tax rate, the after-tax return is 0.03 × (1 − 0.40) = 0.018, or 1.80%.

questions.stem: The expected after-tax return on an equity holding that earns both dividends and price appreciation is most likely:

options.A: The pre-tax return less both tax rates, halved.
options.B: The dividend and appreciation shares of return, each taxed at its own rate.
options.C: The pre-tax return multiplied by one minus the sum of the two tax rates.

rationales.A: Subtracting tax rates from a return mixes two different units, and halving the result assumes the return splits evenly between dividends and price appreciation no matter what the actual proportions are. The weights on the two components are p_d and p_a, which are observed inputs, not a fixed 50/50 split, and each component's tax has to be applied as a proportion of that component's return.
rationales.B: Expected after-tax return on equity is r_at = p_d × r_pt × (1 − t_d) + p_a × r_pt × (1 − t_cg), where p_d is the proportion of return attributed to dividends, p_a is the proportion attributed to price appreciation, t_d is the dividend tax rate, and t_cg is the capital gains tax rate. The pre-tax return is split into its two sources and each source is taxed at the rate that applies to it, which matters because dividends and realized gains are usually taxed differently. For a stock paying no dividends (p_d = 0, p_a = 1) with an 8% pre-tax return and a 25% capital gains rate, the after-tax return is 0.08 × (1 − 0.25) = 0.06, or 6.00%.
rationales.C: Applying one minus the sum of the two rates taxes the entire return at the combined rate, as though every unit of return were hit by the dividend tax and the capital gains tax at once. Each rate applies only to its own share of the return, weighted by p_d and p_a, so the two rates are never added together. With an 8% return that is entirely price appreciation, a 15% dividend rate and a 25% gains rate, this form would give 0.08 × (1 − 0.40) = 4.80% instead of the correct 6.00%.

questions.stem: The after-tax standard deviation assumption for an asset class is most likely:

options.A: The pre-tax standard deviation, unadjusted.
options.B: The pre-tax standard deviation multiplied by one minus the tax rate.
options.C: The pre-tax standard deviation multiplied by one plus the tax rate.

rationales.A: Taxes do affect the dispersion of returns, so leaving volatility unadjusted overstates the risk of a taxable portfolio. Because tax is proportional to the return, it truncates both tails of the return distribution rather than shifting it: the good outcomes are taxed away in part and the bad outcomes are cushioned by the tax benefit of the loss. Using pre-tax volatility in an after-tax optimization therefore feeds the optimizer a risk input that is too high.
rationales.B: After-tax standard deviation is σ_at = σ_pt × (1 − t). Taxes truncate both the high and the low end of the distribution of returns, muting the dispersion and producing lower highs and higher lows. Losses are muted by the same (1 − t) adjustment because the investor receives the economic benefit of a capital loss, which can be offset against gains. The result is that a taxable portfolio's after-tax volatility is lower than its pre-tax volatility, by the same proportion that applies to the return.
rationales.C: This has the wrong sign: multiplying by (1 + t) raises volatility above the pre-tax figure, implying that tax widens the distribution of outcomes. Tax does the opposite. The government takes a share of the gains and absorbs a share of the losses through the offset of a capital loss against gains, so the after-tax distribution is compressed, not stretched, and the adjustment factor must be less than one.

questions.stem: For a taxable asset owner, the appropriate treatment of correlation assumptions in an after-tax optimization is most likely:

options.A: Scaling them down by the tax rate, as volatilities are scaled.
options.B: Setting them to zero, since after-tax returns are uncorrelated.
options.C: Leaving them unadjusted.

rationales.A: Volatility scales with (1 − t), but correlation does not need the same treatment. Correlation is a standardized measure: the tax haircut shrinks each asset's return and each asset's standard deviation in the same proportion, so it cancels out of the ratio. Applying a (1 − t) factor to correlations as well would double-count the tax effect and understate how closely the asset classes still move together after tax.
rationales.B: Tax is proportional to returns, so after-tax co-movements mirror pre-tax co-movements; they do not disappear. Two asset classes that rose and fell together before tax still rise and fall together after tax, just with the amplitude of each move reduced by (1 − t). Treating after-tax returns as uncorrelated would make the portfolio look far better diversified than it is.
rationales.C: Correlation assumptions need not be adjusted when modeling asset allocation choices for the taxable asset owner. Taxes are proportional to return, so after-tax co-movements are the same as pre-tax co-movements and the correlation inputs carry over unchanged. In practice this means the after-tax optimization changes two of the three inputs — expected return is scaled by (1 − t) and standard deviation is scaled by (1 − t) — while the correlation matrix is used as it stands.

questions.stem: For a taxable investor, a mid-frontier asset mix optimized on an after-tax basis, compared with the same mix optimized pre-tax, most likely shows:

options.A: Less in high-yield bonds and more in equities.
options.B: No change at all.
options.C: No equities at all.

rationales.A: A representative mid-frontier portfolio shifts from roughly 25% investment-grade bonds, 26% high-yield bonds and 49% equity on a pre-tax basis to roughly 38% investment-grade bonds, 7% high-yield bonds and 55% equity once taxes are modeled. High-yield bonds carry the heaviest tax burden, because almost all of their return is ordinary-income coupon taxed annually, which cuts their after-tax attractiveness sharply. Investment-grade bonds are taxed at the same rate but are less risky and show lower correlation with equity, so they continue to play the important risk-reduction role and take over most of the fixed-income weight. Equity, whose return comes largely from deferred and preferentially taxed capital gains, gains weight.
rationales.B: Mid-frontier portfolios change materially once taxes enter the optimization. Expected returns and standard deviations are both scaled by (1 − t), and the relevant t differs across asset classes because interest, dividends and realized gains are taxed differently. Asset classes whose return is mostly ordinary income lose more than asset classes whose return is mostly deferred capital gains, so the relative ranking of the inputs changes and the optimizer produces a different mix.
rationales.C: Equities increase rather than disappear. The heavy ordinary-income taxation of high-yield bonds pushes the after-tax frontier toward the more tax-efficient asset class, and equity is the most tax-efficient of the three because its return is largely unrealized appreciation that is deferred and then taxed at capital gains rates. An after-tax optimization raises the equity weight in the mid-frontier mix.

questions.stem: The case for including a tax-inefficient asset class in an optimal after-tax asset allocation most likely rests on:

options.A: Its higher pre-tax return fully offsetting the tax drag.
options.B: The interaction of after-tax returns, after-tax risk, and correlations.
options.C: Its after-tax correlations falling in proportion to the tax rate.

rationales.A: There is no assurance that a pre-tax return premium offsets the tax drag. A tax-inefficient asset class is one whose return is taxed heavily, annually, or at ordinary income rates, and nothing guarantees that its gross return is large enough to leave a competitive after-tax return. The case for holding it rests on its diversification contribution, not on guaranteed compensation for the tax it attracts.
rationales.B: The optimal after-tax asset allocation depends on the interaction of after-tax returns, after-tax risk, and correlations. If an asset class or strategy is tax inefficient, it can still play a diversifying role in an optimal after-tax asset allocation provided it offers sufficiently low correlations with the rest of the portfolio. Because the tax adjustment scales expected return by (1 − t) and standard deviation by (1 − t) while leaving correlations unchanged, the asset's diversification benefit survives the tax haircut even when its after-tax return does not look attractive on its own. After-tax portfolio optimization is what settles the question, by weighing all three inputs jointly rather than screening on after-tax return alone.
rationales.C: Taxes scale after-tax returns and after-tax risk, but correlations are not mechanically reduced in proportion to the tax rate. Correlation is standardized, so the proportional tax haircut cancels out of it and the correlation inputs carry over from the pre-tax assumptions unchanged. Whether a tax-inefficient asset adds value depends on the joint interaction of after-tax returns, after-tax risk and those unchanged correlations, not on any automatic improvement in diversification.

questions.stem: Compared with those of a tax-exempt portfolio of similar risk profile, the rebalancing ranges of a taxable portfolio most likely should be:

options.A: Wider.
options.B: Narrower.
options.C: The same.

rationales.A: Because after-tax volatility is less than pre-tax volatility, σ_at = σ_pt × (1 − t), while correlations remain the same, it takes larger asset class movements to materially alter the risk profile of a taxable portfolio. Rebalancing ranges for a taxable portfolio can therefore be wider than those of a tax-exempt portfolio with a similar risk profile. The wider ranges have a second benefit: they reduce the frequency of trading and, with it, the amount of taxable gains realized.
rationales.B: Narrower ranges would multiply taxable realization events, so the direction is wrong. Each rebalancing trade in a taxable account can trigger a capital gain, and the tax paid is a permanent reduction in the portfolio's compounding base. Tightening the ranges would increase trading frequency at exactly the point where trading is most costly, and it is not required on risk grounds, because after-tax volatility is already lower than pre-tax volatility.
rationales.C: The tax treatment differs, so the ranges should too: wider for the taxable portfolio. Two things drive the difference. After-tax volatility is lower, σ_at = σ_pt × (1 − t), while correlations are unchanged, so a given percentage drift away from target does less to the taxable portfolio's risk profile; and rebalancing a taxable portfolio realizes capital gains, which a tax-exempt portfolio does not have to pay for.

questions.stem: A tax-exempt investor monitors a ±10% rebalancing range around a target allocation. For an otherwise equivalent taxable investor facing a 25% tax rate, the equivalent after-tax rebalancing range is closest to:

rationales.A: This is far too wide. It comes from applying the tax rate as a direct multiple rather than through the (1 − t) relationship: the correct conversion is R_at = R_pt / (1 − t) = 0.10 / 0.75 = 13.3%, not 0.10 / 0.40 or any similar form that produces 25%. The equivalent range widens only modestly at a 25% tax rate.
rationales.B: This narrows the range rather than widening it, by multiplying by (1 − t) instead of dividing: 0.10 × (1 − 0.25) = 0.075, or 7.5%. The (1 − t) factor scales after-tax returns and after-tax volatility downward, but the rebalancing range is being restated from an after-tax basis back to the same gross return perspective as the tax-exempt investor's range, which requires dividing by (1 − t). The taxable investor's equivalent range is wider, not tighter.
rationales.C: The equivalent after-tax rebalancing range is R_at = R_pt / (1 − t) = 0.10 / (1 − 0.25) = 0.10 / 0.75 = 0.1333, or 13.3%. The ±10% rebalancing range for the tax-exempt investor becomes a ±13.3% rebalancing range for the taxable investor when viewed and monitored from the same gross return perspective. Broader rebalancing ranges reduce the frequency of trading and, consequently, the amount of taxable gains realized.

questions.stem: For a taxable asset owner, strategic asset location is a tax-reduction strategy that most likely involves:

options.A: Holding less tax-efficient assets in accounts with more favorable tax treatment.
options.B: Diversifying holdings across tax jurisdictions.
options.C: Holding all assets in taxable accounts.

rationales.A: Strategic asset location is the placement of less tax-efficient assets in accounts with more favorable tax treatment, such as retirement savings accounts. As a general rule, assets eligible for lower tax rates and deferred capital gains treatment should first be allocated to the taxable accounts, which points to equities there, while taxable bonds and high-turnover trading strategies should generally be located in tax-exempt or tax-deferred accounts. The asset allocation itself is unchanged; only the account each holding sits in changes, which is why location can add after-tax value without altering the portfolio's risk profile.
rationales.B: Location in this context refers to the type of account an asset is held in, not the country or tax jurisdiction the investor holds it from. Spreading holdings across jurisdictions is a different decision, with its own withholding tax and treaty consequences, and it does nothing to exploit the difference in tax treatment between an investor's taxable, tax-deferred and tax-exempt accounts.
rationales.C: This is the opposite of strategic asset location. Putting everything in taxable accounts forfeits the shelter that tax-exempt and tax-deferred accounts provide, and it is exactly the assets with the heaviest annual tax burden — taxable bonds and high-turnover strategies — that lose the most from being held there. The strategy is to differentiate between account types, not to collapse everything into one.

questions.stem: The general rule for locating assets across a taxable investor's account types most likely holds that:

options.A: Bonds belong in taxable accounts.
options.B: Each asset class belongs in every account type equally.
options.C: Equities belong in taxable accounts and taxable bonds in tax-deferred accounts.

rationales.A: This reverses the recommendation. Taxable bonds generate interest income that is taxed annually at ordinary income rates, with no deferral and no preferential rate, so they are the holding that benefits most from sitting inside a tax-exempt or tax-deferred account. Equities, whose return is largely unrealized appreciation taxed later and at capital gains rates, are the ones that can be held in the taxable account at relatively little cost.
rationales.B: The rule is specific and differentiated, not uniform. Equal distribution across account types ignores the fact that asset classes are taxed differently: an asset whose return is annual ordinary income is hurt far more by being held in a taxable account than one whose gains are deferred and taxed at a preferential rate. Spreading every asset class evenly across the accounts gives up the whole after-tax benefit that asset location exists to capture.
rationales.C: The general rule is that the portion of a taxable asset owner's assets eligible for lower tax rates and deferred capital gains treatment should first be allocated to the investor's taxable accounts. Equities should generally be held in taxable accounts, because they benefit from capital gains rates and from the deferral of tax until a gain is realized, and because an unrealized gain can ultimately receive favorable treatment. Taxable bonds and high-turnover trading strategies, whose returns are taxed annually as ordinary income, should generally be located in tax-exempt and tax-deferred accounts, where that annual tax drag is sheltered.

questions.stem: An exception to the general rule for asset location is most likely to apply to:

options.A: Assets held for near-term liquidity needs.
options.B: All foreign investments.
options.C: High-net-worth investors.

rationales.A: One important exception to the general rule regarding asset location applies to assets held for near-term liquidity needs. Because tax-exempt and tax-deferred accounts may not be immediately accessible without a tax penalty, a portion of the bond allocation may be held in a taxable account when its role is to fund near-term consumption requirements rather than long-term growth.
rationales.B: Foreign domicile is not the basis of the exception. Where an asset is issued says nothing about whether the investor can reach the proceeds without penalty, and the exception turns on near-term accessibility of the account, not on the geography of the holding.
rationales.C: Wealth level is not the basis of the exception. The carve-out applies to assets earmarked for near-term consumption whatever the investor's net worth; a high-net-worth investor with no near-term liquidity need follows the general rule.

questions.curriculum_ref: Strategies to Reduce Tax Impact — liquidity exception

questions.stem: Tax-loss harvesting most likely involves:

options.A: avoiding realized losses to preserve capital.
options.B: realizing losses to offset capital gains elsewhere.
options.C: swapping bonds in a ladder to lower duration.

rationales.A: Tax-loss harvesting is the intentional realization of losses, not their avoidance. An investor who declines to realize a loss keeps the unrealized position but forgoes the offset against realized gains, and so forgoes the tax saving the technique exists to capture.
rationales.B: Tax-loss harvesting is intentionally trading to realize a capital loss, which is then used to offset a current or future realized capital gain in another part of the portfolio, thereby reducing the taxes owed by the investor.
rationales.C: Swapping bonds within a laddered portfolio to shorten duration is a different technique. It manages interest rate exposure, and any tax consequence is incidental rather than the purpose of the trade.

questions.curriculum_ref: Strategies to Reduce Tax Impact — tax-loss harvesting

questions.stem: For a tax-deferred account whose assets grow tax-free but are taxed on distribution, after-tax value is most likely pre-tax market value:

options.A: left unadjusted.
options.B: multiplied by one minus the expected income tax rate.
options.C: multiplied by one plus the expected income tax rate.

rationales.A: Tax-deferred accounts do carry an embedded tax liability, so leaving pre-tax market value unadjusted overstates the wealth actually available to the investor. The stated balance cannot be consumed in full because the distribution itself triggers the income tax.
rationales.B: After-tax value is v_at = v_pt × (1 − t_i), where v_at is after-tax value, v_pt is pre-tax market value, and t_i is the expected income tax rate upon distribution. Because these assets cannot be distributed, and therefore consumed, without incurring the tax, the tax burden is inseparable from the economic value of the assets.
rationales.C: Multiplying by one plus the tax rate has the wrong sign: it inflates the account by the tax rather than deducting it. The tax reduces what can ultimately be consumed, so the correct multiplier is (1 − t_i), a number below one.

questions.curriculum_ref: Strategies to Reduce Tax Impact — Equation 5

questions.stem: An investor inherits a taxable portfolio to be managed with the same asset classes and the same risk tolerance as her existing tax-deferred portfolio. The most appropriate allocation for the taxable portfolio is most likely to:

options.A: shift equity-like risk from high-yield bonds and dividend equity to total return equity.
options.B: hold the inheritance in cash until the tax rules change.
options.C: match the tax-deferred portfolio's allocation exactly.

rationales.A: The most appropriate recommendation holds roughly 30% investment-grade bonds, no high-yield bonds, no dividend-income equity, and about 70% total return equity. High-yield bonds and dividend-income common stock strategies are tax-disadvantaged in a taxable portfolio because their return arrives largely as currently taxed income. Shifting that equity-like risk into the total return (capital gain) strategy raises the after-tax return. Given the lower after-tax volatility of equity, a higher equity allocation may be justified without exceeding her risk level, and the investment-grade bonds still play the risk-reduction role.
rationales.B: Parking the inheritance in cash is not the recommendation. It abandons the portfolio's return objective while waiting on an event that may not occur; the adjustment called for is a shift of equity-like risk away from the tax-disadvantaged high-yield bond and dividend-income strategies into a capital gain strategy.
rationales.C: Matching the tax-deferred allocation ignores the two accounts' different tax treatment. A taxable setting penalizes tax-inefficient assets such as high-yield bonds and dividend-income equity, so identical weights do not deliver identical after-tax outcomes even at the same risk tolerance.

questions.stem: An investor holds investment-grade bonds, high-yield bonds, dividend-income common stock, and total return common stock across a taxable account and a tax-exempt retirement account. The most appropriate asset location is most likely to:

options.A: randomize the holdings across the two accounts.
options.B: place all but the total return stock in the retirement account.
options.C: place all four holdings in the taxable account.

rationales.A: Randomizing placement is not a strategic recommendation. Asset location is decided by the tax character of each holding's return, so an arbitrary split forfeits after-tax value that costs nothing to capture.
rationales.B: The investment-grade bonds, the high-yield bonds, and the dividend-income common stock all belong in the tax-advantaged retirement account, while the total return (capital gain) common stock belongs in the taxable account. Tax-disadvantaged assets, whose return comes as currently taxed interest or dividend income, go in the tax shelter; capital-gain-eligible assets go in the taxable account, where they benefit from lower capital gains rates and from deferral until the gain is realized.
rationales.C: Holding everything in the taxable account wastes the tax shelter. The interest on the bonds and the dividend income would be taxed annually at the higher income rate, which is exactly the burden the retirement account exists to defer or eliminate.
