drills.los_text: recommend and justify revisions to an asset allocation given change(s) in investment objectives and/or constraints

questions.stem: The three broad categories of circumstances that may trigger a special review of the strategic asset allocation policy are most likely:

options.A: Peer performance, benchmark rebalancing, and index reconstitution.
options.B: A change in goals, constraints, or beliefs.
options.C: Quarter-end, year-end, and month-end.

rationales.A: Peer performance, benchmark rebalancing, and index reconstitution are implementation and monitoring matters. None of them is one of the three categories that call for a special review of the policy itself.
rationales.B: The three broad categories are a change in goals, such as business conditions affecting the sponsoring entity or personal circumstances that alter risk appetite or risk capacity; a change in constraints, such as time horizon, liquidity, asset size, or regulatory change; and a change in beliefs, meaning the investment beliefs and the guiding principles built on them.
rationales.C: Calendar dates are not the basis for a special review. Periodic affirmation that the allocation remains appropriate is sound practice, but a review of the policy is triggered by a change in goals, constraints, or beliefs rather than by the turn of a month or quarter.

questions.stem: Institutional asset owners should most likely revisit the asset allocation policy through a formal study:

options.A: only if the sponsoring entity is dissolved.
options.B: at least monthly or quarterly.
options.C: at least every fifth year, with annual affirmation.

rationales.A: A review timed to the dissolution of the sponsoring entity serves no purpose, because the study exists to keep the allocation suited to the needs of an operating asset owner. Reviews should take place while the entity is operational and the allocation can still be changed to effect.
rationales.B: A formal asset allocation study is a substantial exercise, involving fresh capital market assumptions, modelling, and governance approval. Running one monthly or quarterly is impractical and unnecessary, since goals, constraints, and beliefs rarely shift that quickly.
rationales.C: Many institutional asset owners typically revisit the asset allocation policy at least once every five years through a formal asset allocation study, and all asset owners should affirm annually that the allocation remains appropriate given their needs and circumstances. Special reviews happen in between whenever goals, constraints, or beliefs change materially.

questions.stem: Comparing the 1984–2014 return environment with conditions in 2015–2016, an asset owner setting a strategic asset allocation most likely concludes that:

options.A: past returns ran above trend and the forward outlook has materially changed.
options.B: expected returns do not affect the optimal allocation.
options.C: the earlier period's favorable conditions were expected to persist.

rationales.A: The two eras differ sharply. The 1984–2014 period combined declining inflation and interest rates from their 1970s and early-1980s highs, strong global GDP growth aided by favorable demographics, productivity gains, rapid growth in China, and extraordinary corporate profit growth; returns over that span came in considerably higher than the long-run trend. The 2015–2016 environment ended those trends, with declining productivity gains, a stalling labor force, and intense competitive pressure, and projections published in 2016 showed that neither the slow-growth nor the moderate-growth scenario came close to the returns of the prior 30 years. An allocation developed in 2010 on the back of the previous 26 years of realized returns would therefore look materially different from one built on current forward-looking assumptions.
rationales.B: Expected returns are a primary input to the optimizer, not an irrelevance. A material shift in the expected return vector reworks the efficient frontier and the optimal weights even when the covariance matrix is unchanged, which is why a change in return beliefs is itself grounds for revisiting the allocation.
rationales.C: The conclusion is the opposite: a regime shift. The tailwinds of falling inflation and interest rates, favorable demographics, and extraordinary profit growth were not expected to carry into 2015–2016, so assuming their indefinite persistence is precisely the error the comparison is meant to expose.

questions.stem: A £500 million university endowment receives a £100 million gift. The endowment most likely should:

options.A: invest the gift in parallel with existing assets without review.
options.B: spend the gift immediately to avoid distortion.
options.C: reassess its asset allocation formally before investing the gift.

rationales.A: Investing the gift in parallel with the existing assets fails to consider the increased earning potential of the larger fund and any spending requirements attached to the donation. It treats a significant change in circumstances as though nothing had changed.
rationales.B: Immediate spending is not a strategic response to an inflow. It converts a permanent increase in the fund's earning power into one-off consumption, and it does nothing to address how the enlarged fund should be positioned.
rationales.C: Pausing to formally reassess the fund's goals, objectives, constraints, and opportunities through an asset allocation study allows the asset owner to consider more broadly how best to maximize this additional wealth. A significant cash inflow changes the earning potential of the fund and may carry spending requirements of its own, both of which belong in the analysis before the money is put to work.

questions.stem: A university that reduces its annual endowment spending policy from 5% of assets to 4% most likely:

options.A: gains latitude to invest in less liquid market segments.
options.B: requires no change to its asset allocation.
options.C: must move the endowment entirely to cash.

rationales.A: Faced with lower payouts, the university endowment may have greater latitude to invest in less liquid segments of the market, because less of the portfolio must be kept available to fund distributions. Decisions as to how and where to invest given this greater flexibility should be made within the framework of an asset allocation study, so that the resulting allocation achieves the optimal trade-off of risk and return.
rationales.B: A material change in the spending policy changes the fund's liquidity needs and its required return, so it should trigger a reassessment rather than leave the allocation untouched. Treating a one-percentage-point cut in payout as irrelevant forfeits the flexibility it creates.
rationales.C: Moving entirely to cash is an over-reaction. A lower payout loosens the liquidity constraint and argues for more scope in the allocation, not for abandoning return-seeking assets that the endowment's perpetual horizon supports.

questions.stem: The 2006 US regulatory changes that mandated a change in the pension liability discount rate most likely triggered:

options.A: Higher equity allocations by US corporate pension plans.
options.B: Widespread de-risking toward liability-hedging allocations.
options.C: No material shift in pension asset allocation behavior.

rationales.A: The allocation response ran toward fixed income rather than equity. Because the mandated discount-rate change raised measured liabilities and therefore required contributions, sponsors had less need to reach for higher investment returns, so they moved toward liability-hedging bonds rather than adding equity risk.
rationales.B: Regulatory changes in the US in 2006 mandated a change in the liability discount rate, which resulted in larger pension contributions. With higher required contributions, there was less need to reach for higher investment returns. Many US corporate pension plans began de-risking, adopting an asset allocation strategy focused on hedging the liabilities in order to reduce contribution volatility.
rationales.C: The change did produce a material and widely observed shift. It catalyzed de-risking across many US corporate plans, with assets moved into liability-hedging allocations specifically to damp contribution volatility and funded-status volatility, so describing the period as one of no behavioral change is inconsistent with what sponsors actually did.

questions.stem: For an underfunded pension plan whose funded status improves, the most appropriate asset allocation policy is most likely:

options.A: No change in allocation.
options.B: A pre-programmed glide path.
options.C: An aggressive increase in equity.

rationales.A: Changes in funded status are exactly the kind of milestone that should drive a change in asset allocation. Holding the allocation fixed as the plan's funding position improves leaves the sponsor carrying risk it no longer needs to take, and forgoes the chance to lock in the improvement.
rationales.B: Certain milestones are reasonable points at which to implement a change in policy, in most instances reducing risk. For pension funds, these milestones are typically related to changes in funded status. Putting an asset allocation policy in place that anticipates them, a glide path that reduces risk, typically equity, as funded status improves, allows the investor to respond more quickly to changing circumstances in a non-reactive and objective manner. Target-date mutual funds are a common example of the same pre-programmed mechanism applied to an individual's horizon.
rationales.C: An improving funded status calls for reducing risk, not adding it. Increasing equity after the funding gap has narrowed re-exposes the plan to the volatility it has just escaped, and does so reactively rather than under a pre-set policy.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund set its long-range asset allocation when petroleum revenues were expected to grow for 25 years, with intergenerational distributions beginning in 20 years. Alternate fuels have since eroded oil exports, net inflows are suspended, distributions are now expected within 5 years, and 40% of assets sit in less-liquid asset classes. The most appropriate response is most likely:

options.A: Reducing the allocation to less-liquid asset classes.
options.B: Retaining the current allocation.
options.C: Increasing the allocation to less-liquid asset classes.

rationales.A: The fund adopted its long-range asset allocation under the expectation of continuing net cash inflows and no immediate liquidity constraints. With the change in circumstances, inflows suspended and distributions pulled forward from 20 years to 5, the need for liquidity has increased significantly. The current allocation puts 40% in less-liquid asset classes such as high-yield bonds, hedge funds, and private equity. Those asset classes, or at least the size of the allocation to them, may no longer be appropriate given the change.
rationales.B: The change in circumstances is material, not incidental. Suspended inflows and a distribution horizon shortened from 20 years to 5 both bear directly on the fund's liquidity needs, so an allocation set under a perpetuity-like assumption cannot simply be carried forward unexamined.
rationales.C: This ignores the new liquidity constraint. Adding to less-liquid holdings to harvest an illiquidity premium moves the portfolio in the opposite direction from the one the shortened distribution horizon requires, and risks forced sales at distressed prices when distributions begin.

questions.stem: A closed defined-benefit pension plan holds US$1.0 billion in assets and is 65% funded, allocated 80% to liability-matching bonds and 20% to equities and real estate, and the sponsor intends eventually to buy annuities to fully address the obligations. The sponsor has just announced a US$15 billion capital investment program and will contribute only the pension minimum for the foreseeable future, so full funding will take at least 10 years. The most appropriate recommendation is most likely:

options.A: Maintaining the current asset allocation.
options.B: Purchasing annuities immediately.
options.C: Conducting a new asset allocation study.

rationales.A: The current allocation is inappropriate given the changed timeline. It was set against an expectation of fuller funding and nearer-term annuitization; with contributions cut to the minimum and full funding at least 10 years away, an 80% liability-matching bond portfolio leaves the plan too dependent on contributions it will not receive.
rationales.B: A materially underfunded plan cannot be annuitized. At 65% funded, buying annuities to settle the obligations would require the sponsor to fund the shortfall in cash, which is precisely what the US$15 billion capital investment program has ruled out for the foreseeable future.
rationales.C: The Investment Committee should conduct a new asset allocation study to address the change in cash flow forecasts. The lower contributions imply the pension plan will need to rely more heavily on investment returns to reach its funding objectives, so a higher allocation to return-seeking assets, both public and private equities, is warranted. The company should also suspend the current private equity liquidation plan until the new study has been completed. A liability-matching bond portfolio remains appropriate, but at less than the current 80%.

questions.stem: New advisers or Investment Committee members joining an asset owner's oversight group most likely should trigger:

options.A: An asset allocation study to orient the new members.
options.B: Immediate allocation changes reflecting their preferences.
options.C: No action related to asset allocation.

rationales.A: As new advisers or members join the Investment Committee, they bring their own beliefs and biases regarding certain investment activities. Conducting an asset allocation study to educate these new members and introduce them to the investment philosophy and process adopted by the organization smooths their integration into the governance system and ensures they have a holistic view of the asset owner's goals and objectives.
rationales.B: Acting directly on the preferences arriving with new members would be reactive and biased. It substitutes individual views for the organization's documented philosophy and process, which is the opposite of the objective, non-reactive governance a formal study is meant to support.
rationales.C: A change in the membership of the oversight group is a valid trigger for reviewing asset allocation. Doing nothing leaves new decision-makers voting on a policy whose rationale they have never been walked through.

questions.stem: A university with declining enrollments that must lean more heavily on its endowment to support operating expenditures most likely should:

options.A: Re-evaluate its asset allocation policy.
options.B: Suspend all endowment distributions.
options.C: Leave its asset allocation unreviewed.

rationales.A: A university experiencing declining enrollments that must lean more heavily on the endowment fund to support operational expenditures is a change in goals that should trigger re-evaluation of asset allocation, because the pattern and size of expected payouts from the endowment have changed. When any such event occurs or is anticipated, the existing asset allocation policy should be re-evaluated.
rationales.B: Suspending distributions would be counterproductive. The endowment is being asked to carry more of the operating budget, not less, so cutting payouts to zero would worsen the very shortfall that prompted the change rather than address the allocation question it raises.
rationales.C: This ignores a material change. A heavier and differently timed draw on the endowment alters its liquidity needs and its required return, both of which are inputs to the allocation decision.

questions.stem: Market behavior during the COVID-19 pandemic most likely illustrates:

options.A: No clear implications for asset allocation.
options.B: Volatile short-run returns alongside stable long-term expectations.
options.C: Long-term expectations tracking short-run market volatility.

rationales.A: The period yields a substantive lesson about separating horizons, namely that violent short-run moves need not be read into long-horizon capital market expectations. Treating it as uninformative discards the clearest recent illustration of that distinction.
rationales.B: While short-term market returns resembled a wild roller-coaster in 2020, with the MSCI ACWI down 34% peak to trough from February to March and then up 70.5% from March to December, long-term return expectations did not change nearly as dramatically. Bond return expectations were lowered because of very low government yields, with the 10-year Treasury near 0.6%, but corporate earnings were generally expected to recover as pandemic disruptions declined. Since end-2021, policymakers and markets have focused on assessing the longer-lasting impacts of the pandemic, inflation being the most topical.
rationales.C: Short-term and long-term expectations are distinct and should not move in lockstep. A 34% drawdown followed within months by a 70.5% recovery is precisely the kind of move that long-horizon expectations are meant to look through; letting them follow such swings would turn the strategic allocation into a momentum strategy.

drills.los_text: discuss the use of short-term shifts in asset allocation

questions.stem: Tactical asset allocation (TAA) is most likely distinguished from strategic asset allocation (SAA) in that:

options.A: SAA sets long-term policy targets and TAA permits short-term deviations from them.
options.B: TAA incorporates the investor's liabilities and SAA is asset-only.
options.C: SAA assumes short-run returns are predictable and TAA assumes a random walk.

rationales.A: Strategic asset allocation, also called policy asset allocation, represents the long-term investment policy targets for asset class weights, while tactical asset allocation allows short-term deviations from those SAA targets. TAA is predicated on a belief that investment returns, in the short run, are predictable, which contrasts with the random walk assumption more strongly embedded in most SAA processes.
rationales.B: The SAA/TAA distinction is about horizon and return predictability, not about the treatment of liabilities. Either can be implemented in asset-only or in liability-relative terms, so liability inclusion does not separate the two.
rationales.C: This reverses the assumptions. TAA is the one predicated on short-run return predictability, while most SAA processes embed a random-walk assumption about returns.

questions.stem: Tactical asset allocation moves are most likely justified by:

options.A: Long-term structural change in the economy.
options.B: Cyclical variation within a secular trend or temporary price dislocations.
options.C: Peer-group benchmarks.

rationales.A: Long-term structural change is a strategic asset allocation consideration. A shift expected to persist over the policy horizon belongs in the SAA targets themselves, not in a short-horizon deviation from them.
rationales.B: Tactical moves might be justified based on cyclical variations within a secular trend, such as the stage of the business or monetary cycle, or on temporary price dislocations in capital markets. The objective of TAA is to increase return, or risk-adjusted return, by taking advantage of short-term economic and financial market conditions that appear more favorable to certain asset classes.
rationales.C: Peer benchmarks are not a justification for tactical deviations. Allocating by reference to what comparable funds hold substitutes relative positioning for a view on short-run conditions, and says nothing about whether an asset class is currently mispriced.

questions.stem: Global tactical asset allocation (GTAA) is best described as:

options.A: The same program as TAA, differing only by fund size.
options.B: An opportunistic strategy exploiting valuation anomalies across asset classes.
options.C: A subset of strategic asset allocation focused on policy weights.

rationales.A: Fund size is not the distinction. GTAA extends tactical allocation across multiple markets globally, exploiting pricing and valuation anomalies among countries as well as among asset classes, which is a difference in opportunity set rather than in scale.
rationales.B: Strategic and tactical asset allocation are both distinct from global tactical asset allocation, which is an opportunistic investment strategy that seeks to take advantage of pricing or valuation anomalies across multiple asset classes, typically equities, fixed income, and currencies.
rationales.C: GTAA is opportunistic and tactical, not a strategic policy subset. It operates through short-horizon deviations driven by perceived mispricing, whereas strategic asset allocation sets the long-term policy weights those deviations are measured against.

questions.stem: Tactical asset allocation decisions are least likely to expressly consider:

options.A: Liabilities or goals.
options.B: Asset class returns.
options.C: Policy portfolio ranges.

rationales.A: Tactical asset allocation is an asset-only approach. Although tactical shifts must still conform to the risk constraints outlined in the IPS, they do not expressly consider liabilities (or goals, in goals-based investing). TAA is likewise not concerned with individual security selection: generating alpha through TAA decisions depends on successful market or factor timing rather than on security selection.
rationales.B: Expected returns of the asset classes are central to TAA rather than absent from it. A tactical shift is made precisely because the short-term return expected for an asset class differs from the long-run return assumption embedded in the strategic asset allocation, so asset class returns are the input the decision turns on.
rationales.C: Policy portfolio ranges are expressly considered. Tactical deviations are permitted only within the upper and lower bounds set around each strategic weight in the IPS, so the policy ranges constrain every TAA decision and cannot be the thing TAA ignores.

questions.stem: A common way to evaluate the success of tactical asset allocation decisions is least likely:

options.A: Evaluating TAA and SAA Sharpe ratios.
options.B: Evaluating the information ratio of TAA excess return.
options.C: Evaluating the number of trades executed.

rationales.A: Comparing the Sharpe ratio realized under TAA with the Sharpe ratio of the SAA is one of the three common evaluation methods, so it is not the exception being sought.
rationales.B: Evaluating the information ratio, or the t-statistic, of the average excess return of the TAA portfolio relative to the SAA portfolio is also one of the three common evaluation methods.
rationales.C: Trade count measures activity, not success: it says nothing about whether the tactical deviations added risk-adjusted return. The three common methods are (1) comparing the Sharpe ratio realized under TAA with the SAA Sharpe ratio, (2) evaluating the information ratio or t-statistic of the average excess return of the TAA portfolio relative to the SAA portfolio, and (3) plotting the realized return and risk of the TAA portfolio against the realized return and risk of portfolios along the SAA's efficient frontier, which is particularly useful for assessing risk-adjusted TAA return.

questions.stem: Relative to holding the policy portfolio, tactical asset allocation decisions are most likely to produce:

options.A: Explicit commissions only.
options.B: Higher trading costs and greater risk concentration.
options.C: Lower overall trading costs.

rationales.A: Costs extend beyond explicit commissions. For a taxable investor, tactical trading can generate additional taxes, for example by realizing short-term gains, and tactical positions can also concentrate risk relative to the policy portfolio. Taxes therefore do not fall equally on tactical and strategic trades, because it is the tactical trade that triggers the realization.
rationales.B: Tactical investment decisions may incur additional costs: higher trading costs and, for taxable investors, additional taxes. Tactical decisions can also increase the concentration of risk relative to the policy portfolio. If the tactical decision is to overweight equities, for example, not only is portfolio risk increased but the diversification of risk contributions is also reduced. This is particularly an issue when the SAA policy portfolio relies on uncorrelated asset classes.
rationales.C: Tactical shifts add trades on top of whatever rebalancing activity is already required; they do not substitute for it, because the portfolio must still be returned toward policy weights when the tactical view is unwound. Higher, not lower, trading costs are the consequence of TAA.

questions.stem: The two broad approaches to tactical asset allocation are most likely:

options.A: Top-down and bottom-up.
options.B: Discretionary and systematic.
options.C: Equity-based and fixed-income-based.

rationales.A: Top-down versus bottom-up describes the direction in which research proceeds, not the TAA taxonomy. The TAA distinction is discretionary, meaning qualitative macroeconomic judgment, versus systematic, meaning rules-based value, momentum and trend signals.
rationales.B: There are two broad approaches: discretionary TAA, which relies on qualitative interpretation of political, economic, and financial market conditions; and systematic TAA, which relies on quantitative signals to capture documented return anomalies that may be inconsistent with market efficiency.
rationales.C: Equities and fixed income are asset classes, not decision frameworks. Either approach to TAA is applied across the whole opportunity set, so splitting TAA by asset class does not describe how the tactical decision is made.

questions.stem: Discretionary TAA is most likely predicated on:

options.A: Buy-and-hold indexing.
options.B: Quantitative factor exposures alone.
options.C: Manager skill in timing short-term market moves.

rationales.A: Buy-and-hold indexing is the opposite of tactical allocation: it holds the strategic weights and makes no short-term deviation from them, so it cannot be the premise on which discretionary TAA rests.
rationales.B: Quantitative factor exposures are the basis of systematic TAA. Discretionary TAA relies on qualitative interpretation of political, economic, and financial market conditions rather than primarily on quantitative signals, so factor exposures alone do not describe it.
rationales.C: Discretionary TAA is predicated on the existence of manager skill in predicting and timing short-term market moves away from the expected outcome for each asset class that is embedded in the SAA. In practice, discretionary TAA is typically used in an attempt to mitigate or hedge risk in distressed markets while enhancing return in positive return markets, that is, to produce an asymmetric return distribution.

questions.stem: Common data inputs to discretionary TAA include valuation ratios (P/E, P/B, dividend yield), term and credit spreads, central bank policy, GDP growth, earnings expectations, and most likely:

options.A: Only fundamental company-level analysis.
options.B: Only historical returns.
options.C: Market sentiment indicators.

rationales.A: Discretionary TAA is broader than firm-level fundamental analysis. The decision is taken at the asset class level and draws on macroeconomic and market-wide information, so company-level analysis alone is not the input set.
rationales.B: Historical returns alone are not sufficient. Multiple sentiment and macroeconomic indicators are used alongside them, including central bank policy, GDP growth, earnings expectations, and term and credit spreads.
rationales.C: Market sentiment is a key discretionary TAA input. It includes margin borrowing, a bullishness and bearishness indicator; short interest, a bearish sentiment indicator, where high short interest may signal capitulation; and the volatility or 'fear' indexes, such as VDAX-NEW in Germany, V2X (VSTOXX) for the euro area, and the VIX in the United States, which measure expected volatility implied by option pricing.

questions.stem: The factors used in systematic tactical asset allocation to capture asset-class-level return anomalies are most likely:

options.A: Book value and market capitalization.
options.B: Corporate governance quality and ESG scores.
options.C: Value and momentum.

rationales.A: Book value and market capitalization are single accounting and size metrics, not the documented anomaly factors. The factors used are structured return spreads built from such metrics, such as the return of value stocks over growth stocks, rather than the raw metrics themselves.
rationales.B: Governance quality and ESG scores are security-selection considerations. Systematic TAA runs on value, the value-minus-growth spread, and momentum, the winners-minus-losers spread, applied at the asset class level.
rationales.C: Value and momentum have been determined to have some level of predictability and persistence at the asset class level. The value factor is the return of value stocks over growth stocks; the momentum factor is the return of stocks with higher prior returns over those with lower prior returns. Both are used for security selection within asset classes and for asset class timing.

questions.stem: A basic trend signal used in systematic TAA is most likely:

options.A: A random walk in prices over the trailing 12 months.
options.B: The most recent 12-month return.
options.C: The average return over the past 30 years.

rationales.A: If asset prices followed a random walk, past returns would carry no information about future returns and trend following would be pointless. A trend signal presumes the opposite: that the recent direction of returns persists and is therefore exploitable.
rationales.B: A basic trend signal is the most recent 12-month return: the expectation is that the direction of the most recent 12-month returns can be expected to persist for the next 12 months. Shorter time frames and different weighting schemes can also be used. Another trend signal is the moving-average crossover, which fires when the moving average over the shorter time frame moves above or below the moving average over the longer time frame.
rationales.C: Averaging returns over 30 years destroys the information the signal is meant to capture: a three-decade mean is dominated by long-run drift and barely moves with recent direction. The signal is the most recent 12-month return, not a multi-decade average.

questions.stem: Carry in currencies uses short-term interest rate differentials to determine which currencies to overweight or underweight. Analogously, carry in commodities most likely uses:

options.A: P/E ratios.
options.B: Roll yields.
options.C: Credit ratings.

rationales.A: A price-to-earnings ratio requires earnings, which a commodity does not have. P/E is an equity valuation measure and cannot form a commodity carry signal.
rationales.B: Carry in commodities compares positive roll yields, which arise under backwardation, with negative roll yields, which arise under contango, to determine which commodities to own or short. For bonds, the analogous signals are yields-to-maturity and term premiums, that is, yields in excess of the local risk-free rate, which indicate the relative attractiveness of different fixed-income markets.
rationales.C: A credit rating assesses the default risk of an issuer. A commodity has no issuer whose creditworthiness could be rated, so ratings are not the commodity carry signal.

questions.curriculum_ref: Short-Term Shifts — carry signals across asset classes

questions.stem: A trend signal is long IG bonds (excess return 3%), short HY bonds (−3%), long DM equity (4%), and short EM equity (−11%). Strategic targets are IG bonds 40%, HY bonds 10%, DM equity 40%, and EM equity 10%, each with a permitted range of ±5%. The recommended tactical allocation is most likely:

options.A: IG bonds 50%, HY bonds 0%, DM equity 50%, EM equity 0%.
options.B: IG bonds 40%, HY bonds 10%, DM equity 40%, EM equity 10%.
options.C: IG bonds 45%, HY bonds 5%, DM equity 45%, EM equity 5%.

rationales.A: These weights move each asset class 10 percentage points from its strategic target and so breach the permitted range of plus or minus 5%: 50% against a 45% maximum for IG bonds and DM equity, and 0% against a 5% minimum for HY bonds and EM equity. The strength of a signal, including the −11% reading on EM equity, does not license a deviation beyond the policy limits.
rationales.B: Leaving the strategic weights unchanged ignores signals that are clear in direction for all four asset classes. The policy constraint is the permitted range of plus or minus 5% around each target, not a prohibition on deviating at all, so the signals justify moving each weight to its limit in the direction indicated.
rationales.C: The tactical decision must be taken in the context of the SAA policy constraints. Although the signals for HY bonds and EM equity are negative, the minimum permissible weight in each is 5%, so neither can be taken to zero. Similarly, although the IG bond and DM equity signals are positive, the maximum permissible weight in each is 45%. Asset classes can be over- or underweighted to the full extent of the policy limits, which gives IG bonds 45% (+5%), HY bonds 5% (−5%), DM equity 45% (+5%), and EM equity 5% (−5%).

drills.los_text: identify behavioral biases that arise in asset allocation and recommend methods to overcome them

questions.stem: Among the behavioral biases most relevant in asset allocation, the group least likely to be included is:

options.A: Loss aversion, illusion of control, and mental accounting.
options.B: Momentum bias, technical analysis anchoring, and support-resistance bias.
options.C: Representativeness bias, framing, and availability bias.

rationales.A: Loss aversion, the illusion of control, and mental accounting are three of the six biases identified as most relevant in asset allocation, so every item in this group belongs on the list rather than off it.
rationales.B: The six behavioral biases most relevant in asset allocation are loss aversion, the illusion of control, mental accounting, representativeness (recency) bias, framing, and availability bias. Momentum bias, technical analysis anchoring, and support-resistance bias are trading and chart-reading heuristics; none of the three appears among the six, which makes this the group that is least likely to be included.
rationales.C: Representativeness (recency) bias, framing, and availability bias are the remaining three of the six, so this group is also fully on the list.

questions.curriculum_ref: Dealing with Behavioral Biases in Asset Allocation

questions.stem: Loss aversion is most likely defined as:

options.A: the inability to distinguish between losses and gains of equal size.
options.B: the asymmetric preference for avoiding losses over acquiring equivalent gains.
options.C: the tendency to prefer realizing losses over realizing equivalent gains.

rationales.A: Loss-averse investors distinguish losses from gains very sharply indeed; that asymmetric weighting of the two is the bias itself. An investor who genuinely could not tell a loss from an equal-sized gain would weight the two identically, which is the symmetric treatment standard mean-variance utility already assumes and the opposite of loss aversion.
rationales.B: Drawing on prospect theory (Kahneman and Tversky), loss aversion is the asymmetric risk preference under which people strongly prefer avoiding losses to acquiring equivalent gains: the pain of a loss is approximately twice as significant as the joy from an equivalent gain. Because the investor's utility is not symmetric around the reference point, this motivates non-normal utility functions and asymmetric optimizers such as mean-CVaR, which penalize downside outcomes rather than variance in both directions.
rationales.C: The pattern runs the other way: loss-averse investors avoid realizing losses, because booking a loss delivers roughly twice the pain that an equal-sized realized gain delivers pleasure. A preference for realizing losses ahead of equivalent gains would describe tax-loss harvesting discipline, not the bias.

questions.stem: Illusion of control — the tendency to overestimate one's ability to influence events — most likely manifests in asset allocation as:

options.A: greater willingness to employ tactical shifts and seek alpha.
options.B: reduced willingness to make any investment decisions.
options.C: sharper forecast calibration from closer attention.

rationales.A: Investors subject to the illusion of control overestimate their control over investment outcomes, which increases their willingness to employ tactical shifts away from the strategic allocation. Manifestations include alpha-seeking behaviors such as attempted market timing via extreme tactical asset allocation and all-in/all-out market calls; reliance on a belief in 'superior resources'; excessive trading, leverage, and short selling; reducing or eliminating asset classes on the basis of non-consensus forecasts; and retaining large, concentrated legacy positions.
rationales.B: The bias increases the appetite for intervention rather than producing decision paralysis. An investor who overestimates his influence over outcomes trades more, not less, and tilts further from the strategic allocation.
rationales.C: Overconfidence rather than better calibration follows. The observed behaviors are extreme tactical shifts, attempted market timing, all-in/all-out trading, and concentrated positioning, all of which reflect forecasts held with more confidence than their accuracy warrants.

questions.stem: The illusion of control bias in asset allocation is most appropriately mitigated by:

options.A: increasing tactical trading frequency to build experience.
options.B: eliminating quantitative analysis in favor of instinct.
options.C: anchoring the allocation on the global market portfolio with strict policy ranges.

rationales.A: Trading more often feeds the bias rather than tempering it. Frequent tactical activity gives the investor repeated occasions to attribute outcomes to his own skill, and the random reinforcement of occasional success strengthens the belief that outcomes are within his control.
rationales.B: The remedy is structure, not instinct. Removing the quantitative discipline strips out exactly the elements that constrain the bias: the global market portfolio as a neutral starting point, long-term return and risk forecasts, and a formal optimization whose constraints keep the result near defensible weights.
rationales.C: The recommended mitigation is to use the global market portfolio as the starting point in developing the asset allocation, building on the CAPM, mean-variance optimization, and efficient market theory. Deviations from that baseline must be thoughtfully considered and rigorously vetted. A formal asset allocation process then supports this discipline through long-term return and risk forecasts, optimization constraints anchored around the asset class weights in the global market portfolio, and strict policy ranges that limit how far tactical conviction can move the portfolio.

questions.curriculum_ref: Behavioral Biases — mitigating illusion of control

questions.stem: Hindsight bias — the tendency to perceive past investment outcomes as having been predictable — most likely:

options.A: Corrects the illusion of control.
options.B: Exacerbates the illusion of control.
options.C: Has no relationship to the illusion of control.

rationales.A: Hindsight bias reinforces the illusion of control rather than correcting it. An investor who remembers past outcomes as having been foreseeable concludes that his judgment was sound, which raises rather than lowers his estimate of his own influence over results.
rationales.B: Hindsight bias, the tendency to perceive past investment outcomes as having been predictable, exacerbates the illusion of control. Believing that events could have been predicted increases confidence in one's ability to predict future events, and that inflated confidence is what drives the tactical shifts, market timing, and concentrated positioning associated with the illusion of control.
rationales.C: The relationship is direct and exacerbating, not absent. The two biases compound: a distorted memory of past predictability supplies the apparent evidence on which the overestimate of control rests.

questions.stem: Mental accounting is most likely defined as:

options.A: the tendency to evaluate each holding relative to its purchase price.
options.B: the tendency to frame outcomes relative to a reference point rather than final wealth.
options.C: the tendency to treat one sum of money differently from another by mental account.

rationales.A: Anchoring on a holding's purchase price is a reference-point effect associated with loss aversion, where the pain of booking a loss against cost basis drives the decision. It is not the definition of mental accounting, which concerns treating sums of money differently according to the account to which they have been assigned, whatever their cost basis.
rationales.B: This describes framing bias, the sensitivity to how outcomes are presented relative to a reference point rather than in terms of final wealth. Framing is a separate one of the six biases relevant in asset allocation; mental accounting is about the segregation of money into accounts, not the presentation of outcomes.
rationales.C: Mental accounting is an information-processing bias in which people treat one sum of money differently from another based solely on the mental account the money is assigned to. An investor may consider a retirement portfolio independently of a child's education portfolio even though the combined asset allocation is suboptimal, and an employee with significant vested stock options may fail to consider that exposure alongside his other assets.

questions.stem: Goals-based investing most likely addresses mental accounting bias by:

options.A: incorporating mental accounting directly into the allocation solution.
options.B: removing the need to verify that the aggregate of sub-portfolios is efficient.
options.C: replacing goal sub-portfolios with a single whole-of-wealth optimization.

rationales.A: Goals-based investing incorporates mental accounting directly into the asset allocation solution. Each goal is aligned with a discrete sub-portfolio, and the investor can specify the acceptable level of risk for each goal. Provided each sub-portfolio lies along the same efficient frontier, the sum of the sub-portfolios will also be efficient. This turns mental accounting from a bias to be corrected into a productive structural approach, since the investor's own segregation of money by purpose becomes the organizing principle of the allocation.
rationales.B: Aggregate efficiency still matters. Only if each sub-portfolio lies along the same efficient frontier will the sum of the sub-portfolios also be efficient, so the check is a condition of the approach working rather than something it dispenses with.
rationales.C: Goals-based investing does the opposite of a single whole-of-wealth optimization. It aligns each goal with a discrete sub-portfolio and lets the investor set the acceptable level of risk for each goal, which is precisely what accommodates the mental accounting the investor already practices.

questions.curriculum_ref: Behavioral Biases — goals-based and mental accounting

questions.stem: A founder-entrepreneur's preference to retain a concentrated position in the company he built, despite its risk, is most likely:

options.A: driven by psychological loyalty to the asset, reinforced by the endowment effect.
options.B: driven purely by tax considerations and therefore always rational.
options.C: irrelevant to the asset allocation decision.

rationales.A: There may be rational reasons for retaining the position, including ownership control, an information advantage, and tax considerations, but the desire to retain the riskier exposure is more often the result of a psychological loyalty to the asset that generated the wealth. This mental accounting bias is further reinforced by the endowment effect, the tendency to ascribe more value to an asset already owned than to another asset one might purchase to replace it.
rationales.B: Tax considerations are acknowledged as one of several rational reasons to retain a concentrated position, alongside ownership control and an information advantage, but the psychological drivers are identified as the more significant explanation in most cases. Treating the preference as purely tax-driven and always rational overstates the rational case and leaves the loyalty and endowment effects unexamined.
rationales.C: The concentration is central rather than irrelevant to the asset allocation decision. A single holding large enough to dominate the risk of total wealth has to be brought into the allocation, whether through diversification, hedging, or deliberate assignment to a lower-priority goal.

questions.stem: In goals-based asset allocation, a client's concentrated stock position is most appropriately accommodated by:

options.A: assigning the position to an aspirational goal.
options.B: ignoring the position when setting the asset allocation.
options.C: prohibiting concentrated positions entirely.

rationales.A: The concentrated stock and the mental accounting bias behind it are accommodated in goals-based asset allocation by assigning the position to an aspirational goal, one the client would like to achieve but is willing to assign a lower probability of success. Lifetime consumption is a high-priority goal that requires a well-diversified portfolio, whereas an aspirational goal such as a charitable gift can reasonably be funded with the concentrated position. Funding a gift to a tax-exempt charity with the appreciated shares could also avoid the capital gains tax altogether.
rationales.B: Ignoring the position ignores real risk. The concentrated holding still contributes volatility and idiosyncratic exposure to total wealth, so an allocation computed as though it were absent understates the client's risk and overstates the diversification of the whole.
rationales.C: An outright prohibition does not work against the client's psychological attachment to the asset that generated the wealth. The practical course is to accommodate the holding within a goal whose lower required probability of success can tolerate it, while funding high-priority goals from diversified assets.

questions.stem: Representativeness (recency) bias is most likely defined as:

options.A: the tendency to reject new information in favor of prior beliefs.
options.B: the tendency to overweight recent observations relative to long-term data.
options.C: the tendency to anchor forecasts on long-term historical averages.

rationales.A: Rejecting new information in favor of previously held views is conservatism bias, which under-reacts to news. Representativeness does the reverse: it over-extrapolates the recent past, treating a short run of observations as representative of the whole distribution.
rationales.B: Representativeness, or recency, bias is the tendency to overweight the importance of the most recent observations and information relative to a longer-dated or more comprehensive set of long-term observations. Tactical shifts undertaken in response to recent returns or news are particularly susceptible to it. Return chasing is a common manifestation, resulting in overweighting asset classes with good recent performance just as their expected returns have fallen.
rationales.C: Anchoring forecasts on long-term historical averages is the opposite tilt, and closer to the discipline that mitigates the bias. Recency bias overweights the newest observations at the expense of the longer-dated record.

questions.stem: The argument that recency bias is not uniformly negative is most likely supported by the fact that:

options.A: random walk, trending, and mean reversion can all be relevant over different horizons.
options.B: recency bias removes the need for a structured asset allocation process.
options.C: recent data keep estimates current, so the bias always improves forecasting accuracy.

rationales.A: Random walk, trending, and mean reversion may be simultaneously relevant to the investment decision-making process, although their effects on asset prices unfold over different time horizons. That is the sense in which recency bias is not uniformly negative: recent data are sometimes genuinely informative, because markets do at times trend or revert rather than follow a pure random walk. What makes the bias harmful is extrapolating the recent past without regard to horizon. The strongest defenses are an objective asset allocation process and a strong governance framework; a formal asset allocation policy with pre-specified allowable ranges constrains the drift that recency bias would otherwise produce.
rationales.B: No such implication follows. Because random walk, trending, and mean reversion may all be simultaneously relevant, judgment about which pattern applies over which horizon remains hard, and that is precisely why a structured, objective asset allocation process with pre-specified allowable ranges is the main defense against recency bias. The bias makes the structured process more necessary, not less.
rationales.C: The bias systematically distorts estimates rather than improving them. The nuance is only that markets sometimes do trend, which makes recent data genuinely relevant over some horizons; that is a long way from a claim that weighting the recent past more heavily always raises forecasting accuracy. Objective processes and governance frameworks exist because the typical effect is distortion.

questions.curriculum_ref: Behavioral Biases — recency bias and market dynamics

questions.stem: Framing bias in asset allocation is most likely illustrated by:

options.A: the same risk shown as standard deviation, VaR, or CVaR prompting different choices.
options.B: asset classes having universal risk properties.
options.C: all portfolios being priced in US dollars.

rationales.A: Framing bias is illustrated by the way the same risk, presented differently, changes the allocation chosen. Viewing expected return and volatility alone — a 6.0% return with an 11.9% standard deviation — many investors gravitate to portfolio P50. Loss aversion, however, means some of those same investors find P50's −18.5% CVaR indicative of a level of risk they are very uncomfortable with. The CVaR frame intuitively communicates a different perspective on exactly the same risk that is already fully described by the standard deviation, namely its downside and tail-risk aspects. Because the frame, not the risk, is what changed, the resulting shift in the allocation decision is framing bias.
rationales.B: Universality of risk properties is not the argument. Risk measures differ in which aspect of a distribution they emphasize, and asset classes do not carry universal risk properties. Framing bias concerns how one given risk is presented to the investor — standard deviation versus VaR versus CVaR — not whether risk behaves identically across asset classes.
rationales.C: Currency framing is not the example. The illustration turns on the choice of risk measure, where standard deviation and CVaR describe the same distribution but communicate it differently. Requiring that portfolios be priced in a single currency is a reporting convention and does not change the perceived risk/reward trade-off.

questions.stem: Framing bias in asset allocation is most likely mitigated by:

options.A: presenting allocation choices from multiple risk/reward perspectives.
options.B: eliminating all quantitative analysis.
options.C: presenting expected returns only.

rationales.A: The framing effect is mitigated by presenting the possible asset allocation choices with multiple perspectives on the risk/reward trade-off. Standard deviation can be supplemented with shortfall probability, tail-risk measures such as VaR and CVaR, historical stress tests, and Monte Carlo simulations, each of which captures and communicates risk more tangibly than volatility alone. Showing several frames at once compels the investor to consider more carefully which outcomes are acceptable and which are not, rather than letting a single presentation of the same risk determine the choice.
rationales.B: The remedy is more quantitative structure, not less: shortfall probability, VaR and CVaR, historical stress tests, and Monte Carlo simulations are added alongside standard deviation. Removing quantitative analysis would leave the investor with fewer perspectives on the same risk and so would leave the framing effect fully intact.
rationales.C: A return-only presentation would exacerbate the bias rather than mitigate it. It is the single-frame view — return and volatility alone, with no shortfall probability or tail-risk measure beside it — that leads investors toward allocations whose downside they would reject once the CVaR frame is shown.

questions.stem: Availability bias is most likely defined as:

options.A: the inability to access certain products because of platform restrictions.
options.B: a mental shortcut that estimates probability from how easily an outcome comes to mind.
options.C: the systematic under-weighting of recent, easily recalled information.

rationales.A: Product access is an operational or platform constraint, not a psychological one. Availability bias is an information-processing bias — a mental shortcut used when estimating probabilities — and it operates regardless of what an investor is able to buy.
rationales.B: Availability bias is an information-processing bias in which people take a mental shortcut when estimating the probability of an outcome based on how easily that outcome comes to mind. Easily recalled outcomes are perceived as more likely than outcomes that are harder to recall. For example, private equity investors who lived through the liquidity squeeze of 2008–09 are likely to express a strong preference for liquidity, assigning a higher probability to such an event recurring than would an investor who had cash available at the time to acquire distressed private equity interests. The same experience, differently recalled, produces different probability estimates and therefore different asset allocations.
rationales.C: The direction runs the other way. Probability estimates track how easily instances come to mind, so recent and vivid information is over-weighted rather than under-weighted; an investor who recalls a liquidity squeeze easily assigns a higher, not a lower, probability to its recurrence.

questions.stem: Familiarity bias, a specific form of availability bias, in asset allocation most likely results in:

options.A: over-diversification across unfamiliar asset classes.
options.B: a home bias toward securities listed on domestic exchanges.
options.C: no observable effect on portfolio composition.

rationales.A: Familiarity concentrates a portfolio in what is already known rather than spreading it into what is not, because the familiar is what comes easily to mind. Over-diversification across unfamiliar asset classes is the opposite of the bias's effect; the documented outcome is a narrower, home-weighted opportunity set.
rationales.B: Familiarity bias stems from availability bias: people tend to favor the familiar over the new or different because of the ease of recalling the familiar. In asset allocation it most commonly results in a home bias — a preference for securities listed on the exchanges of one's home country. Concentrating portfolio exposure in home-country securities, particularly where home-country capital markets are small, results in a less diversified and less efficient portfolio. The bias can be mitigated by using the global market portfolio as the starting point for the allocation, so that any home-country overweight becomes a deliberate, documented decision rather than a default.
rationales.C: The effect is well documented as home bias — an overweight to securities listed on home-country exchanges at the cost of diversification and efficiency, especially where those markets are small. Composition is visibly altered, which is why the global market portfolio is recommended as the neutral starting point.
